text: Numbers are the easy part. Real datasets are full of names typed with stray spaces, emails in mixed case, phone numbers in five different formats, and addresses that need to be split apart. If you can't clean text, you can't join tables reliably — ben at example dot com with a trailing space will never match ben at example dot com without one. pandas gives you a whole toolbox for this through the dot-s-t-r accessor, which applies Python string operations to every value in a column at once.

Here's illustrative raw data, the kind you'd get straight from a web form. Notice the extra spaces around some names, inconsistent capitalization everywhere, and one missing name entirely. The email column has mixed case and a trailing space; the phone column uses parentheses, dashes, dots, and spaces, all for the same kind of number.

Dot-s-t-r dot strip removes leading and trailing whitespace. Dot-lower, dot-upper, and dot-title change the case. Chain them together, since each one returns a Series that supports dot-s-t-r again — strip, then lower, turns that messy trailing-space email into a clean lowercase one in a single line.

For the names, we also need to collapse the double space sitting inside Cara Singh. Str dot replace with a regular expression does it — backslash-s-plus means one or more whitespace characters, replaced with a single space. Chain strip, that replace, and title together, and Cara double-space Singh becomes a clean Cara Singh. Always pass regex equals True or regex equals False explicitly to str dot replace, because the default has changed between pandas versions. Missing values pass straight through untouched — the missing name stays missing rather than causing an error.

Str dot split breaks each string at a separator. Split each email at the at-sign, then take dot-s-t-r bracket 1 to pick the second piece — the domain. Counting those domains shows three at example dot com, one at shop dot io, one at example dot org — a quick way to spot personal versus business addresses. The same bracket syntax slices too — name dot s-t-r bracket colon 3 grabs just the first three characters.

Str dot contains returns True or False per row, ready to use directly as a filter mask — does the name contain the letter a, ignoring case. One trap: contains on a column with missing values returns a missing result for those rows, which breaks filtering outright. Pass na equals False so missing text counts as no match instead of blowing up the filter. Also remember contains treats the pattern as a regular expression by default, so a plain dot matches any character — pass regex equals False for literal text.

Str dot extract pulls out the parts of a string that match the groups in parentheses. Extract from each email with a pattern that captures everything before the at-sign as one group and everything after as another, and you get back two clean columns: the username and the domain, side by side. Each set of parentheses in the pattern becomes its own output column. You don't need to master regular expressions today — backslash-d is a digit, backslash-s is whitespace, plus means one or more, and a dot means any character, and that covers most data work.

Now a worked example: standardizing phone numbers. The phones use parentheses, dashes, dots, and spaces — strip out everything that isn't a digit with str dot replace on backslash-D, then check the length. The cleaned digits come out as straight ten-digit numbers, and the first three characters give you the area code — 512, 617, 512, 303, 617. Every length here is 10, meaning every number is complete. In real data, a length of 9 or 11 is a red flag worth investigating — checking a rule like this on purpose is exactly the seed of the validation work coming in Chapter 5.

To recap: the dot-s-t-r accessor runs string methods across a whole column at once. Clean with strip, lower, title, and replace; break strings apart with split and slicing; search with contains, always using na equals False; and pull out patterns with extract. Standardized text is what makes joins and counts actually trustworthy. Next chapter: data cleaning, beginning with a systematic look at missing data.
